verses.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men:

a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

If a man fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not filled with good, and moreover he has no burial; I say, that a stillborn child is better than he:
for it comes in vanity, and departs in darkness, and its name is covered with darkness.
Moreover it has not seen the sun nor known it. This has rest rather than the other.
Yes, though he live a thousand years twice told, and yet fails to enjoy good, don’t all go to one place?
All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
For what advantage has the wise more than the fool? What has the poor man, that knows how to walk before the living?
Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
Whatever has been, its name was given long ago; and it is known what man is; neither can he contend with him who is mightier than he.
For there are many words that create vanity. What does that profit man?
For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he spends like a shadow? For who can tell a man what will be after him under the sun?

footnotes.content: The Preacher opens here with something I've watched unfold many times: a person blessed with much, yet somehow carrying the weight of it all. It's a riddle the world doesn't understand—abundance that burdens the soul rather than filling it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What a cruel paradox: a man has riches enough to meet every desire, yet cannot enjoy them—someone else eats the fruit of his labor. In my own season, I've learned the only real wealth is the capacity to receive what God gives us day by day, not the hoard we think we own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred children, a long life—the measure of earthly success. Yet the Preacher says if the soul remains empty of good, unfed by anything that truly sustains it, then even this abundance becomes hollow. Long life without purpose or rest is its own kind of poverty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stillborn child, the Preacher says, comes and goes in darkness—and finds rest in that darkness. It's a hard saying, but I hear what he means: a life that comes into this world grasping only at vapor has no true name, no legacy worth grieving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stillborn never saw the sun or knew its warmth, yet in that ignorance finds more rest than the man who lives long without finding meaning. There's a mercy in not knowing what you've missed, I suppose—but the truer mercy is in learning to receive what the Lord gives moment by moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even if a man lived two thousand years and never enjoyed anything good—never tasted the fruit of his own work—where does it leave him? The grave levels all of us. I've come to see that the years we're given matter not by their number, but by whether we've learned to rest in the hand of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All our labor feeds the mouth, yet the appetite never fills. I've watched this truth play out—the more we reach, the more we want. Jesus knew this hunger too, and He offers us food of a different kind: His own flesh and blood, the only sustenance that satisfies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What advantage has the wise man over the fool? What does the poor man gain from knowing how to live? In the end, both of us have the same hunger, the same limited time. Wisdom without peace is just another form of want.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Better to see what's in front of us than to waste our days chasing every wandering desire that dances at the edge of our vision. Yet even this preference—this choice to see rather than to crave—is itself vanity, the Preacher reminds us, unless the Lord is at the center of what we're seeing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Everything has a name already, given long ago. The patterns repeat; we cannot contend with One mightier than ourselves. There's humility in this—and peace too, once you stop imagining you could win a quarrel with the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So many words promising so much, and yet they only multiply emptiness. I've lived long enough to see how speech without substance leaves us exhausted. The words that matter are few, and they often come down to this: trust, rest, and return to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who knows what is good for us? The Preacher asks this in his weariness, but readers today hear an echo in it: we spend our days as a shadow, grasping at answers we cannot hold. And yet the Lord holds us. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful for a grace that doesn't ask us to know the future—only to rest in His hands today.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
